keySentence: Emil showed that working together and thinking clearly solves problems.

facts.Page story text 1 (draft, teacher check: When the police finally arrested Grundeis they found the stolen money still in his possession. Emil was able to describe exactly how much money there was and in which pocket it had been hidden. The policeman was impressed by how clearly and carefully Emil had thought about everything he knew. And he was impressed by the organized group of children who had all watched the thief so patiently. Emil told the policeman that he could not have done any of it without his new friends helping him. The policeman smiled and said that Emil was exactly right and that this was how difficult problems got solved. Emil showed that working together and thinking clearly solves problems.
facts.Page story text 2 (draft, teacher check: The police were initially skeptical when a crowd of children arrived at the bank insisting that a man was a thief. Children made these kinds of claims sometimes and they were usually based on misunderstanding or imagination or both. But Emil's account was so precise and so calmly delivered and so completely consistent with every detail that it demanded attention. He had the denomination of each note, the position in which they had been pinned inside his jacket, and the sequence of events. And he had witnesses — children who had watched Grundeis all night from every angle and who corroborated everything Emil said. The combination of clear individual thinking and well-organized collective observation produced something that the police could not dismiss. Grundeis was arrested and the money was returned and Emil learned something that he would carry with him for the rest of his life. Emil showed that working together and thinking clearly solves problems.
facts.Page story text 3 (draft, teacher check: The resolution of Emil and the Detectives offers Kästner's most complete statement of the novel's central argument. The argument is that competence — real, practical competence that changes the situation — requires two things working together. The first is clear individual thinking: the ability to observe accurately, reason soundly, and communicate precisely under pressure. The second is effective collective action: the ability to organize, trust, divide labor, and sustain effort across time and uncertainty. Emil provides both — clear thinking about what happened and what is needed, and the ability to build and maintain a working team. Neither quality alone would have been sufficient — clear thinking without collective action would have produced a frustrated individual. Collective action without clear thinking would have produced a disorganized crowd that lost the thief in the first half-hour. The combination is what makes Emil's victory not just satisfying as a story but instructive as an example of how problems actually get solved. Emil showed that working together and thinking clearly solves problems.
